statement: In one randomized, double-blind crossover trial in a laboratory, 18 healthy adults who had used cannabis before but not in the previous 30 days (the completers of 22 randomized; Zamarripa et al., 2023) each ate, in random order on days at least a week apart, a placebo brownie, a brownie with a THC-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC, no CBD) and a brownie with a CBD-dominant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD), and swallowed a cocktail of five probe medicines, including the sedative midazolam, 30 minutes later in every session (study conditions only). Compared with the THC-dominant brownie, the CBD-dominant brownie was associated with higher blood levels of THC and of 11-OH-THC, a substance the body makes from THC (peaks 14.8 against 8.2 and 53.9 against 4.5, units not printed in the text: about 1.8 and 12 times higher, editors' arithmetic), and with stronger effects, most of them unwanted. Peak rises from each session's baseline on 0–100 scales, rated by the participants in double-blind sessions, were larger for drug effect (72.8 against 59.2), unpleasant (38.6 against 19.6), feeling sick (26.1 against 11.6), memory trouble (37.8 against 27.4) and difficulty with routine tasks (46.7 against 30.3); scores on an arithmetic task and a divided-attention task were worse (P = .049 and .04), and heart rate rose more (by 25.4 against 10.1 beats a minute). Pleasant and liking ratings did not differ significantly, and anxious (23.9 against 13.3), paranoid (23.4 against 12.0) and sleepy (42.6 against 21.0) ratings, though higher than after placebo, did not differ significantly from the THC-dominant brownie. The placebo brownie with the probe medicines changed no effect measure significantly. Effects were followed for 24 hours: the strongest drug effect came later on average (2.9 against 2.1 hours after the probe medicines; not tested statistically) and total THC exposure (area under the curve) was about 2.5 times higher (editors' arithmetic), but how long the stronger effects lasted is not given in the parts of the paper that could be read. In these conditions the CBD-dominant extract did not soften THC's effects, which the authors present as contrary to common claims that CBD dampens THC's unwanted effects; whether the difference came from CBD, from the extract's other cannabinoids or from changed levels of the probe medicines, which the paper does not report, cannot be told, and the trial tested one amount of CBD, eaten in the same brownie as the THC, in adults who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days; smoked or vaped cannabis was not tested. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one lab trial, 18 healthy adults who had not used cannabis for at least a month ate brownies with THC alone or with the same THC plus a large amount of CBD. With CBD, blood THC was higher, and people felt the drug more, felt sicker, had more trouble with memory and simple tasks, and had a faster heartbeat, without liking it more. Other test medicines, including a sedative, were given in every session, so it is not certain what caused the difference, and only one amount of CBD, eaten in a brownie, was tested.
population: 18 healthy adults aged 18 to 50 (11 men, 7 women; mean age 30) with past cannabis use but none in the 30 days before the first session (mean 124 days since last use), completers among 22 randomized, at the Johns Hopkins Behavioral Pharmacology Research Unit, United States
exposure: A brownie with a CBD-dominant whole-plant extract (20 mg THC with 640 mg CBD; the extract also held about 2% CBC and 1% CBG), followed 30 minutes later by a cocktail of five probe medicines (caffeine, omeprazole, losartan, dextromethorphan, midazolam) (study conditions only)
comparator: The same participants after a brownie with a THC-dominant extract carrying the same nominal THC dose (20 mg THC, no detectable CBD) and after a placebo brownie, each with the same probe cocktail
outcome: Plasma THC, 11-OH-THC and THC-COOH; peak change from baseline in self-ratings on the Drug Effect Questionnaire (0–100), cognitive task performance and heart rate over 24 hours
magnitude: CBD-dominant against THC-dominant extract, mean (SD): THC peak 14.8 (5.5) against 8.2 (4.0), area under the curve 84.9 (29.38) against 33.3 (16.9); 11-OH-THC peak 53.9 (22.6) against 4.5 (1.9), area 349.0 (137.1) against 34.0 (16.4); all P < .001; units not printed in the text (editors' arithmetic: THC peak about 1.8 and area about 2.5 times, 11-OH-THC peak about 12 and area about 10 times higher). Peak change from baseline on 0–100 ratings, CBD-dominant against THC-dominant: drug effect 72.8 against 59.2; unpleasant 38.6 against 19.6; sick 26.1 against 11.6; dry or red eyes 28.8 against 15.9; memory 37.8 against 27.4; routine tasks 46.7 against 30.3 (all Tukey P < .05); anxious 23.9 against 13.3, paranoid 23.4 against 12.0, sleepy 42.6 against 21.0 (not significant). Paced serial addition -22.7 against -6.6 correct (P = .049); divided-attention tracking error 32.7 against 15.9 (higher is worse; P = .04); heart rate +25.4 against +10.1 beats a minute (P = .001). Time of peak drug effect 2.9 against 2.1 hours (not tested). Many printed Cohen's d values for the effects do not match the printed means and SDs (some, such as drug effect, memory and routine tasks against the THC-dominant extract, do), and several printed intervals include zero beside P < .05; the d values are not used.

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns (card sc_zamarripa_2023): only completers analysed after 4 of 22 randomized participants dropped out and were replaced, with the reasons in a figure that could not be viewed; 36 outcomes without correction across outcomes; the abstract, text and table disagree on several effect results, and many printed effect sizes do not match the printed data.

indirectness.note: The probe cocktail, including the sedative midazolam and dextromethorphan, was taken in every session and its levels under each extract are not reported, so part of the extra impairment may come from it; the CBD-dominant extract also carried other cannabinoids; one large oral CBD amount, in healthy adults who did not use cannabis regularly.

imprecision.note: 18 people; the two task differences were at P = .049 and .04, and the printed intervals for the effects cannot be relied on.

publication_bias.note: Registered trial (NCT04201197); these are secondary outcomes.

grade.reasoning: Randomized, double-blind crossover comparisons start high (METHODS §6.3); rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, giving very low for the claim as worded, whose weakest necessary link is the stronger effects. The rise in blood THC and 11-OH-THC on its own is large, objective and precise and would rate low (high, minus risk of bias and indirectness). Worded as an association because the two extracts differed in more than CBD and the probe medicines may have contributed. Status single study: other trials of CBD with THC, mostly inhaled, a 2019 systematic review (Freeman et al.) and a 2026 meta-analysis of blood THC with CBD (Chester et al.) are on the reading list and have not been read; the answer may become contested when they are.
